sources.text:
Why Do Leaves Change Colour?

In many countries, green leaves turn yellow, orange or red in autumn, and then they fall. Why does this happen?

A leaf is green because it has a green material called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll helps the tree to make food from sunlight, air and water. In spring and summer, the tree makes a lot of chlorophyll, so the green colour covers the other colours in the leaf.

In autumn, the days get shorter and the nights get longer. With less sunlight, the tree stops making new chlorophyll. The old chlorophyll slowly breaks down, and the green colour disappears. Now we can see yellow and orange. These colours were in the leaf all summer, but the green colour hid them.

Some trees, like maples, also make a new red colour in autumn. Their leaves are brightest after sunny days and cool nights.

Next, a thin wall grows where the leaf joins the branch, and the leaf falls. Thin leaves full of water could freeze in a cold winter, so the tree drops them.

In Hanoi, the big leaves of the Indian almond tree (cây bàng) turn red in winter. I think these red leaves are the most beautiful thing in our city.

sources.text:
How Do Bats Find Food in the Dark?

Hello! Today's question is: how can a bat catch insects at night, when it is too dark to see well?

Many bats use sound. While a bat is flying, it makes very high sounds. Most of these sounds are too high for people to hear. When a sound hits an insect, it bounces back to the bat. This returning sound is called an echo.

The bat listens to the echo carefully. The echo tells the bat where the insect is. The bat also notices how long the echo takes to come back. This tells it how far away the insect is. Then the bat flies quickly and catches its dinner.

Finding things with echoes like this is called echolocation. But not all bats do it. Some big fruit bats find their food mainly with their eyes and their good sense of smell.

So next time you see a bat at night, remember: it is listening to the dark!

sources.text:
Why Do Volcanoes Erupt?

Deep under the ground, it is extremely hot. In some places, part of the rock melts. Melted rock under the ground is called magma.

Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises. It often collects deep under a volcano, in a place called a magma chamber.

Magma has gas in it, a bit like the gas in a bottle of fizzy drink. Deep underground, the heavy rock above presses on the magma, so the gas stays inside. But when the magma rises near the surface, there is less pressure. The gas comes out and makes bubbles. The bubbles grow bigger and push the magma up. When the push is strong enough, the magma breaks through the ground. This is an eruption. When magma comes out of a volcano, we call it lava.

Not all eruptions are the same. Some magma is runny, like soup. The gas escapes easily, so the lava pours out and flows like a red river. Kilauea in Hawaii usually erupts this way. Other magma is thick and sticky, like honey. The gas is trapped, and the pressure builds up. As a result, the volcano explodes and throws ash high into the sky. Mount St. Helens in the USA had thick magma like this, and it exploded in 1980.

sources.text:
Hi, I'm Dr Linh, and I am a volcano scientist. People often ask me, "Can you tell the exact day a volcano will erupt?" The honest answer is no. But we can see warning signs.

Every day, my team watches a volcano for three signs. First, we count small earthquakes. When magma moves up under the ground, it breaks rock, and this makes many small earthquakes. Second, we measure the ground. When magma collects under a volcano, the ground can rise a little, like a balloon. Third, we check the gas. When magma moves closer to the surface, the gas coming out of the volcano can change.

If we see all three signs getting stronger, we tell the people who live nearby. Then they can leave their homes in time. Our job is not to stop eruptions. Our job is to keep people safe.

sources.text:
The Never-Ending Journey of Water

Some of the water in your glass may once have been in a cloud, a river or the sea. Water moves around the Earth again and again. This journey is called the water cycle.

The journey starts with the Sun. The Sun heats the water in seas, rivers and lakes. Some of the water turns into a gas called water vapour. We cannot see water vapour, but it is in the air all around us. This change from liquid water to gas is called evaporation. Plants help too: they let out water vapour from their leaves.

Warm air with water vapour rises. High in the sky, the air is cold, so the water vapour cools down. It changes back into tiny drops of water. This is called condensation. Millions of these tiny drops make a cloud.

Inside the cloud, the drops bump into each other and join together. They grow bigger and heavier. When they are too heavy to stay in the air, they fall as rain. Sometimes they fall as snow or hail instead. This is called precipitation.

The rain flows into rivers and back to the sea, or it soaks into the ground. Then the Sun heats the water again, and the journey starts again.

sources.text:
Hi, I'm Mai. Yesterday was a very hot day, and the air felt wet, so I made a glass of iced water. After ten minutes, I saw something strange. There were lots of small drops of water on the outside of the glass! The table under the glass was wet too.

At first, I thought the glass had a hole. But the water inside did not go down. So where did the drops come from?

My teacher explained it to me. The air around us has water vapour in it. When the warm air touched the cold glass, the water vapour cooled down. It changed into tiny drops of liquid water on the glass. This is called condensation.

The same thing happens in the sky. High up, the air is cold, so water vapour cools and makes tiny drops. That is how clouds start. My cold glass showed me the beginning of a cloud!

sources.text:
Why Does the Ground Shake?

The ground under our feet feels still. But the outside of the Earth is not one solid piece. It is broken into huge pieces called plates, like the cracked shell of a boiled egg.

The plates move very slowly, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Some plates move apart, some push into each other, and some slide past each other.

The edges of the plates are rough, so they often get stuck. The plates keep pushing, but the edges cannot move. Energy builds up in the rocks, like a ruler that you bend more and more. Then, suddenly, the rocks slip, like the ruler springing back. The stored energy travels out in all directions as waves. These are called seismic waves. When the waves reach the surface, the ground shakes. This is an earthquake.

The crack where the rocks slip is called a fault. The place on the surface right above the start of the earthquake is called the epicentre. The shaking is usually strongest near the epicentre.

Many earthquakes are very small, and people do not feel them. After a big earthquake, smaller ones called aftershocks often follow.

sources.text:
What should you do if the ground starts to shake? Remember three words: Drop, Cover, Hold On.

First, drop down onto your hands and knees. This stops you from falling over.

Next, cover your head and neck with your arms. If there is a strong table or desk near you, get under it. Things can fall from shelves and walls, so protect your head.

Then, hold on to the table and stay there until the shaking stops.

Do not run outside while the ground is shaking, and do not stand in a doorway. Stay away from windows, because the glass can break.

If you are outside, move to an open place, away from buildings, trees and electric wires. Then drop down and stay there.

When the shaking stops, wait for an adult to tell you what to do next.

sources.text:
Venus: Earth's Hot Twin

Venus is the second planet from the Sun. At its closest, Venus comes nearer to Earth than any other planet, and it is almost the same size as Earth. That is why people sometimes call it Earth's twin. But Venus is a terrible place to visit.

Venus is the hottest planet in our Solar System. The temperature on its surface is about 465 degrees Celsius. That is hot enough to melt some metals! Mercury is closer to the Sun, but Venus is hotter. Why?

The answer is its atmosphere. The air on Venus is very thick, and it is mostly carbon dioxide. This thick air traps the heat from the Sun, like a heavy blanket. The heat cannot escape, so the planet stays extremely hot, day and night.

The air on Venus is also very heavy. If you stood on Venus, the air would press on you more than 90 times harder than the air on Earth. Its thick clouds are made of acid, too.

Venus spins very slowly, and it spins in the opposite direction from most planets. One day on Venus is longer than one year there! Venus has no moons.

sources.text:
Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun. It is about half the size of Earth. Mars looks red because its rocks and dust have iron in them, and the iron has rusted.

Mars is much colder than Earth, and there are two reasons. First, Mars is farther from the Sun, so it gets less heat. Second, its atmosphere is very thin. Thin air cannot hold the heat, so the heat escapes into space. The temperature can go from about 20 degrees Celsius on a summer afternoon down to about minus 150 degrees in the coldest places.

A day on Mars is a little longer than a day on Earth, about 24 and a half hours. But a year on Mars is almost two Earth years long. Mars has two small moons, called Phobos and Deimos.

Scientists have sent robots to explore Mars, but no person has been there yet.
